newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Taiwan wonders if WTO marathon will ever end.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taiwan wonders if WTO marathon will ever end.

text.p: Taiwan is frustrated by a long struggle to join the top international free trade club and now rival China's own membership bid has made entry even more complex.
In 1990, a vigorous Taiwan launched its bid to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, predecessor of the current World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Back then, few might have guessed Taiwan's ambition to join the club, which aims to remove trade barriers, would become a gruelling marathon of seven years -- or even longer.
The venerable "Asian tiger" is one of the world's major trading partners and says its long run should be rewarded with WTO membership -- and that politics should stay out of the way.
Officials express deep frustration at perceived interference by communist-ruled China, which faces its own obstacles to WTO entry but insists that it must accede before Taipei.
Taiwan's oft-postponed deadline has been pushed back to the end of 1997, although many analysts call that over-optimistic.

"It is evident that the process is influenced by the international political environment, and that there is linkage between mainland China's accession and ours," said Chiang Pin-kung, Taiwan's economic tsar as head of the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development.
"It is our feeling that Taiwan and mainland China's applications should be treated separately, but political reality...is far beyond our control," Chiang said in an interview.
Hemmed in by Beijing's view of Taiwan as a renegade province ineligible for international recognition, Taipei seeks WTO entry not as a sovereign but as a customs territory, Chinese Taipei.

Although Taiwan has close economic and trade links with most countries, the wealthy island of 21 million people is recognised diplomatically by only 30 nations. Pressure from Beijing has kept Taiwan out of most international organisations.

Taiwan had a trade surplus of US$14.704 billion in 1996, up 81.3 percent from 1995. The island's gross domestic product showed 6.83 percent annual growth in the first quarter, with the full-year 1997 GDP forecast at 6.24 percent
MEMBER NATIONS TOO DEMANDING
China is a major obstacle, but not the only one.
Officials complain that some WTO members -- chiefly the United States -- have ignored the steady opening of Taiwan's markets and the dismantling of its state monopolies.

"We've already gone a long long way with our market-opening measures," said Chiang. "However, there are some sectors in which liberalisation simply cannot proceed as broadly and swiftly as some members have requested."

"Unfortunately, some members have not been willing to take such factors into account, but have pressed and pressed for satisfaction of their full demands, which is why negotiations have yet to be finally concluded even after 170 rounds.
"The United States is always very demanding," he added.

The United States and European Union top the list of eight WTO members with which Taiwan still must complete bilateral negotiations. Agreements have been reached with the other 18 members that sought such talks.
The latest round of U.S. talks ended in May with little progress. Negotiators leave for Geneva soon for renewed talks with Europe, but are in no mood to make concessions.
"We understand clearly if we want to join the WTO, we need to play by the game rules set by the WTO members," Taiwan's chief WTO negotiator, Lin Yi-fu, told Reuters in an interview.

"We understand we need to pay an entrance fee in order to join the club," said Lin, director general of the Board of Foreign Trade. "But we've already made all possible commitments. There isn't much room left for further concessions."
HUGE ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL IMPACT
Officials acknowledge that a drastic opening of long-protected industries -- chiefly agriculture and services as well as wine and tobacco -- would be a tough political battle at home.
Some critics question whether Taiwan is paying too high a price in its drive to attain its place in the WTO.

"The most troubling thing to local industries about Taiwan's WTO bid is that nobody knows how far the government will go in making market-opening concessions and tariff reductions," a local newspaper said in a recent commentary.
A government report calculated WTO membership could cost Taiwan 270,000 jobs, almost doubling its 300,000 unemployed.
Officials pledge measures to minimise the huge economic and social impacts, but caution that Taiwan must endure "growing pains" in order to upgrade its industry and economy.
A separate report published by the Council for Economic Planning and Development was more optimistic.
"The WTO entry will inevitably have some impact on Taiwan's job market in the short term...But it will benefit the economy as a whole in the long run," the council report said.
The council reckoned that membership could create 100,000 jobs for Taiwan over a decade.
